issues.legal_issue: A legislative bill was validly passed despite the official record omitting an entry that the final motion was put and carried.
material_facts: The Speaker certified on the printed bill soon after the legislative proceedings that the bill had been passed.
The later printed proceedings omitted any statement that the final motion had been put to a vote or carried.
The recorded speeches at the final stage supported passage, and no member opposed the bill.
The Speaker signed the proceedings months after certifying the bill.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not establish that the bill had not been passed; the Speaker’s certification was accepted and the omission was treated as an accidental procedural lapse.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Speaker’s contemporaneous certification and parliamentary practice, as discussed in Craies’ Statute Law and May’s Parliamentary Practice. Das J. additionally held that any omission was an irregularity of procedure cured by article 212 of the Constitution; the later confirmation under the former rule 115 did not displace the earlier certification.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_enacted_law and speaker_certified_passage and later_record_omitted_final_vote and recorded_debate_supported_passage

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enacted_law: A person challenging an enacted law alleged that the legislature had not validly passed it.
predicates.speaker_certified_passage: The presiding officer certified the bill as passed soon after the legislative proceedings.
predicates.later_record_omitted_final_vote: A later official record did not state that the final motion had been put and carried.
predicates.recorded_debate_supported_passage: The recorded debate at the final stage showed support for passage and no opposition.

issues.definition: When an enacted law is challenged, a prompt certification of passage, together with a supportive recorded debate, can establish valid passage despite a later record omitting the final vote.

issues.legal_issue: A bill reserved by a Governor for presidential consideration and assented to by the President need not first receive the Governor’s assent or be submitted to the President a second time.
material_facts: The legislative assembly passed the bill and the Governor reserved it for the President’s consideration.
The President assented to the bill.
The bill was not first assented to by the Governor and then reserved again for presidential consideration.
issues.conclusion: The presidential assent was sufficient; the Constitution did not require a preliminary gubernatorial assent or a second reservation and assent.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed articles 200, 201, 31(3) and 31(4) of the Constitution together. A bill reserved by the Governor may become law through the President’s assent, and requiring the President to assent twice to the same bill would be a meaningless formality.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the validity of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.governor_reserved_passed_bill: The Governor reserved a bill passed by the legislature for presidential consideration.
predicates.president_assented_to_reserved_bill: The President assented to the bill that had been reserved.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition law was enacted through reservation of the passed bill and presidential assent, that process was sufficient without an earlier gubernatorial assent or a second presidential assent.

issues.legal_issue: The legislature was competent to enact a law acquiring proprietary land rights as part of land-tenure reform.
material_facts: The law acquired proprietary rights in estates, villages and lands and transferred them to the State.
The law aimed to eliminate intermediaries between the State and cultivators and to bring cultivators into direct contact with the State.
issues.conclusion: The legislature had competence to enact the acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the legislation fell within the legislative subject of acquisition under entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.law_transfers_proprietary_land_rights_to: The law transfers proprietary land rights to the State.

issues.definition: A challenged law transferring proprietary land rights to the State as an acquisition is within legislative competence over acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: Eliminating intermediaries and establishing direct relations between cultivators and the State constitutes a public purpose for land acquisition.
material_facts: The law sought to eliminate intermediary holders between the State and cultivators.
It aimed to establish direct contact between cultivators and the Government, improve tenants’ land status, and place village affairs and common lands under democratic village management.
issues.conclusion: The law served a public purpose and the objection that it did not was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its reasoning in the Bihar case and held that land-tenure reform establishing direct relations between cultivators and the State was for the general public benefit.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.law_aims_to_eliminate_land_intermediarie: The law seeks to remove intermediary holders between the State and cultivators.
predicates.law_directly_benefits_cultivators: The law seeks to improve cultivators’ position or establish direct relations between them and the State.

issues.definition: When an acquisition law removes land intermediaries and is directed to the benefit of cultivators, the acquisition serves a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that statutory compensation is inadequate is barred where the acquisition law is protected from Part III challenges, and a positive compensation entitlement is not illusory merely because it is substantially below the property’s asserted value.
material_facts: The law prescribed compensation calculated by reference to net income and provided that net income could not be reduced below five per cent of gross income.
The petitioner asserted that the compensation for property worth substantially more would be much smaller and payable in instalments.
The law had received presidential assent and was included in the Ninth Schedule.
The compensation formula produced a positive amount rather than zero or a negative amount.
issues.conclusion: The compensation could be described as grossly inadequate, but its adequacy was not justiciable; the compensation was not illusory because the law provided for a positive payment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on article 31(4), articles 31-A and 31-B, and its reasoning in the Bihar case. Article 31(4) barred an objection based on article 31(2) where its conditions were met, while articles 31-A and 31-B supplied further protection from Part III challenges. The Court distinguished inadequate compensation from no compensation or illusory compensation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenged a law that acquires private property.
predicates.acquisition_law_is_constitutionally_prot: The acquisition law has received the constitutional protection that bars relevant Part III objections.
predicates.law_provides_positive_compensation: The law provides for a compensation payment greater than zero.

issues.definition: When a protected acquisition law provides positive compensation, a challenge to the amount’s adequacy is barred and the payment is not illusory merely because it is low.

issues.legal_issue: The sequence of land-revenue measures and acquisition legislation did not establish that the acquisition law was a fraud on the Constitution.
material_facts: The legislature had enacted earlier measures that increased land revenue or withdrew exemptions before enacting the acquisition law.
The earlier measures were within the Government’s power, and most preceded the Constitution’s commencement.
The Court found no evidence that the measures were enacted with a fraudulent design to defeat constitutional compensation requirements.
The acquisition law itself provided for positive compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on its reasoning in the Bihar case and held that the sequence of legislation could have been undertaken in good faith; the mere existence of revenue changes and acquisition legislation did not prove a fraudulent design.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.prior_revenue_measures_preceded_acquisit: The government changed land-revenue obligations before enacting the acquisition law.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fraudulent_design: The evidence did not establish that the measures were devised to defeat constitutional guarantees.

issues.definition: When revenue measures precede an acquisition law but there is no evidence they were designed to evade constitutional guarantees, the sequence does not establish fraud on the Constitution.

issues.legal_issue: Leaving the amount and timing of compensation instalments to rules did not make the acquisition law unenforceable or amount to an improper delegation of essential legislative power.
material_facts: The law authorized compensation to be paid in one or more modes, including instalments or bonds.
The statute left details of instalment payments to rules made under it.
The statute also required an interim payment if full compensation was not paid within the specified period.
The statute fixed the compensation framework rather than leaving the essential legislative choice to the executive.
issues.conclusion: The delegation objection was rejected, and the absence of instalment details in the statute did not make it unenforceable; rules could prescribe those details, subject to challenge if their application abused the delegated power.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on its reasoning in the Bihar case and on the statutory provisions empowering rule-making and requiring interim compensation. It distinguished implementation details from essential legislative functions.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and statute_sets_compensation_framework and payment_details_are_left_to_rules and statute_provides_interim_payment

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of property.
predicates.statute_sets_compensation_framework: The statute itself establishes the framework for determining compensation.
predicates.payment_details_are_left_to_rules: The statute leaves the detailed method or schedule of payment to rules.
predicates.statute_provides_interim_payment: The statute requires an interim payment if full compensation is not made within the prescribed time.

issues.definition: When a statute fixes the compensation framework and provides for interim payment, leaving payment details to rules does not by itself make the delegation improper or the scheme unenforceable.

issues.legal_issue: Protection of a scheduled statute under article 31-B is independent of article 31-A and can apply to scheduled property even if it is not an estate within article 31-A’s definition.
material_facts: The challenged Act was specified in the Ninth Schedule.
Some acquired villages were conceded not to fall within the relevant land-tenure definition of an estate.
The petitioners argued that article 31-B was merely illustrative of, and limited by, article 31-A.
issues.conclusion: Article 31-B operated independently of article 31-A, and the challenged Act could not be questioned under Part III in respect of the villages outside article 31-A’s estate definition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed articles 31-A and 31-B as independent protections and relied on King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee, holding that the analogy to the phrase “without prejudice to the generality” did not make article 31-B merely illustrative. Article 31-B specifically protected the scheduled Acts.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A person challenged a law listed for constitutional protection.
predicates.law_is_listed_for_constitutional_protect: The challenged law is expressly included in the constitutional list of protected laws.
predicates.acquired_property_falls_outside_estate_d: The acquired property does not fall within the applicable definition of an estate.

issues.definition: When a challenged law is expressly listed for constitutional protection, that protection applies independently even to acquired property outside the relevant estate definition.

issues.legal_issue: A covenant recognizing property as a ruler’s private property did not guarantee that the property could never be acquired, and a dispute arising from the covenant was not justiciable.
material_facts: A merger covenant recognized the properties as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
The acquisition law treated the properties as private property and sought to acquire them on that basis.
The petitioners relied on the constitutional assurance concerning rulers’ personal rights, privileges and dignities.
The dispute concerned the effect of the covenant.
issues.conclusion: The covenant did not prevent acquisition of the private property, and the covenant-based dispute was not justiciable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied articles 362 and 363 of the Constitution. Article 362 did not guarantee the perpetual existence of property recognized as private property, and article 363 barred judicial determination of disputes arising from the covenant. Das J. also stated that the assurance related to personal rights, privileges and dignities qua ruler and did not bar acquisition of private property.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenged a law that acquires property.
predicates.merger_covenant_recognizes_private_owner: A merger covenant recognizes the property as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
predicates.acquisition_treats_property_as_private: The acquisition proceeds on the basis that the property is privately owned.
predicates.dispute_depends_on_covenant: The asserted bar to acquisition depends on interpreting or enforcing the merger covenant.

issues.definition: Recognition of private ownership in a merger covenant does not itself immunize property from acquisition, and a challenge dependent on the covenant is not justiciable.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of land through compulsory acquisition is not excluded from legislative competence merely because the measure is described as nationalization.
material_facts: The law transferred proprietary land rights to the State.
The petitioners argued that nationalization was a separate legislative subject and that general acquisition did not cover it.
The challenged measure operated through compulsory acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The nationalization argument was rejected; the acquisition was within the relevant legislative subject.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the cited passage from Stephen’s Commentaries, read in full, did not support excluding nationalization from acquisition, and noted that properties had been nationalized in various countries through powers of compulsory acquisition. It applied entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: A person challenged a law that compulsorily acquires property.
predicates.law_transfers_property_to_state_by_compu: The law transfers property to the State through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.challenge_labels_measure_nationalization: The challenger argues that the transfer is nationalization rather than acquisition.

issues.definition: Calling a compulsory transfer of property nationalization does not, by itself, take the measure outside legislative competence over acquisition.
